issue.title: Expand sparse `FixedString` and `Decimal` columns to full ones in one pass
issue.body:
<!--
Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need.

Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN   (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch)
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN
-->
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/129692


### Changelog category (leave one):
- Performance Improvement


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Expanding a sparse `FixedString`, `Decimal` or `DateTime64` column to a full one (for `GROUP BY`, `JOIN`, sorting and most functions) now fills the default values in one pass and copies only the non-default ones, which reduces the CPU time of such queries by up to 13%.

### Description

A column is stored sparse when at least `ratio_of_defaults_for_sparse_serialization` (0.9375) of its values are defaults. `ColumnDecimal` (`Decimal32` to `Decimal256`, `DateTime64`, `Time64`) and `ColumnFixedString` had no `createWithOffsets`, so turning such a column into a full one (`ColumnSparse::convertToFullColumnIfSparse` and the sparse path of `IFunction`) used the generic implementation: a virtual `insertFrom` per value and `insertManyFrom` per run of defaults, which for `FixedString` copies the default row by row.

Both overrides follow `ColumnVector::createWithOffsets`: one exact allocation, one fill of the default, one checked copy per non-default value. `Nullable` forms get it through `ColumnNullable`. Suggested by @ Algunenano in the review of #129692; the implementation follows the patch posted there by @ snelheidai (https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/129692#issuecomment-6756293474).

Exploratory local runs: clang-22 release, 100M rows with 10% non-default values, single-threaded wall time, median of 8 paired base/patched runs [93% interval], shared host:

| Query | Sparse column |
|---|---|
| `GROUP BY fs` | -13.6% [-13.9, -12.9], -13.7% [-14.0, -13.0] |
| `d64 + 1 > 500` | -10.1% [-13.2, -9.3], -11.3% [-12.7, -10.4] |

Two runs pairing each query with the same query on a non-sparse table confirm both: `GROUP BY fs` -14.7%, -14.2% (non-sparse -0.9%, -0.5%), `d64 + 1` -12.4%, -12.6% (non-sparse -2.1%, -2.6%). A `bitNot(fs)` filter got equally faster on the non-sparse table, so it is not counted. Multi-threaded timings on this host are within its noise; the new performance test `sparse_column_fixed_size.xml` measures them in CI.

A new test compares sparse and non-sparse copies of the same data (`FixedString`, `Decimal32` to `Decimal256`, `DateTime64`, their `Nullable` forms, and functions with a non-default result); mutating any branch of the new functions makes it fail. Query results are identical and peak memory does not grow in the A/B runs.

issue.title: Stop waiting in the `bytes_to_delay_insert` delay of a `Distributed` table once the `INSERT` is cancelled
issue.body:
<!--
Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need.

Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN   (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch)
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN
-->
Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/130442
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/129890


### Changelog category (leave one):
- Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Fixed `KILL QUERY` and a graceful server shutdown not cancelling an `INSERT` into a `Distributed` table that waits because its pending bytes are above `bytes_to_delay_insert`. Such an `INSERT` waited up to `max_delay_to_insert`, so with `max_delay_to_insert` above `shutdown_wait_unfinished` the server exited forcefully and lost the rows held in `Buffer` tables and in the asynchronous insert queue.

### Description

On 26.10, with `max_delay_to_insert` above `shutdown_wait_unfinished`, a graceful restart while an `INSERT` into a `Distributed` table waits in the `bytes_to_delay_insert` delay force-exits and loses the rows held in `Buffer` tables and the asynchronous insert queue. With the issue's setup the stop took 122.5 s and kept 0 of 100 `Buffer` rows; with this PR, 4.7 s and 100 of 100.

`StorageDistributed::delayInsertOrThrowIfNeeded` sleeps while the pending bytes stay above the threshold and never reads the query's cancellation. At shutdown `killAllQueries` cancels the pipeline, but the sleeping `DistributedSink` ignores it, the connection outlives `shutdown_wait_unfinished`, and `Server::main` exits before `ContextSharedPart::shutdown` flushes anything.

`DistributedSink::consume` now passes its cancellation flag to the delay. A cancelled `INSERT` leaves the loop and skips the post-delay `DISTRIBUTED_TOO_MANY_PENDING_BYTES` throw, like the shutdown exit of #129890, and the client still gets `QUERY_WAS_CANCELLED`. It does not throw on cancellation: `killAllQueries` also cancels an asynchronous insert flush, and its rows were already acknowledged to `wait_for_async_insert = 0` clients. Trade-off: in the default background mode a cancelled delayed `INSERT` still queues its block, like any block consumed when the cancel lands. The `parts_to_delay_insert` delay of `MergeTree` does not loop and is not changed.

Validation: four new cases in `test_buffer_flush_on_shutdown` (a client `INSERT` and a refreshable materialized view `APPEND TO` the table at shutdown, `KILL QUERY`, an asynchronous insert flush in the delay at shutdown). The first three fail on master (forced stop, `KILL QUERY` timeout) and pass with the fix; the last fails if the cancel throws.

issue.title: Terminate on exceptions in the workload scheduler thread

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Pull request with bugfix, not backported by default

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Workload scheduler and resource management: CPU/IO/memory scheduling, concurrency control, worklo...

issue.body:
### Changelog category (leave one):
- Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Fixed hangs of workload scheduling. A query using CPU scheduling with separate `MASTER THREAD` and `WORKER THREAD` resources could stop the scheduler thread of a resource when a workload was changed concurrently, after which queries and workload DDL waited forever; such a query now fails instead. A workload named like `p1_fair` could leave its sibling workloads detached, so their queries waited forever.


### Description
An exception escaping a workload scheduler thread was swallowed by the global thread pool: the thread exited silently, and queued requests and later workload DDL waited forever. Now the scheduler thread never dies silently:

- Both scheduler loops are `noexcept`, so an exception escaping them terminates the server. `MemoryTracker` does not throw in this thread (`LockMemoryExceptionInThread`, accounting is kept), nor in the drain of `stop`.
- A failure while modifying the scheduling hierarchy (create, update or delete a workload node) used to reach the DDL caller, which only logged it and left the hierarchy half-modified. It now terminates the server.

Two throws that could reach the scheduler thread are fixed:
- `PriorityPolicy` and `PrecedenceAllocation` keyed their children by name, so a workload named like the internal fair node next to it (`p<N>_fair`) failed the update and left workloads detached. They are keyed by node now.
- `CPULeaseAllocation::grant` and `CPUSlotsAllocation::grant` enqueue the next request, possibly into the other resource's queue (master vs. worker), which may have been purged; that throws `INVALID_SCHEDULER_NODE`. The allocation now fails instead, as if the queue had failed the request.

### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
...

### Description
`Fast test (arm_darwin)` on #124968 failed in `02833_local_udf_options` and `05227_allow_executable_tables_ddl_does_not_run_script` in the same second, both with `Pipe read timeout exceeded 10000 milliseconds` from `ShellCommandSource`: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/41830596067/job/126624255903. In 05227 the error comes from the positive control `SELECT * FROM t_gate` over `Executable('marker.sh', 'TSV')`, not from the `ExecutablePool` part. On 2026-11-10 `05047_selected_rows_executable_loop_double_count` failed the same way in `Fast test (arm_darwin)` of another PR: https://s3.amazonaws.com/clickhouse-test-reports/praktika.html?PR=115356&sha=7e664bf8c2ec4224b9a16ebf9ba2118640bc5cea&name_0=PR&name_1=Fast%20test%20%28arm_darwin%29.

The per-read bound `command_read_timeout` (default 10000 ms) also covers the child's startup. On that runner both children (`udf.sh`, `marker.sh`) were spawned at 14:11:10 UTC and finished about 13 s later, while the other tests of that window ran at their usual speed. The macOS runner has a recurring tail close to the bound: over 30 days the slowest passing run is 9.78 s for 02833 and 8.72 s for 05227, against 1.53 s and 2.16 s on Linux.

None of the three tests checks the 10 s default, so this sets `command_read_timeout = 30000` for the 02833 UDF and for every `Executable`/`ExecutablePool`/`executable()` script read in 05227 and 05047. Other executable tests share the 10 s default but have not failed, so they are unchanged. 30 s stays below the Fast test's 60 s per-test limit, so a hung script still fails with the timeout error. Same approach as #113004.

Validation: with scripts that sleep 12 s (UDF, table and table function), the old definitions fail with `Pipe read timeout exceeded 10000 milliseconds` and the new ones return their rows; setting the UDF key to 3000 reports `3000 milliseconds`, so the value is read. All three tests pass 50/50 with randomized settings and 5/5 with the Fast test flags, with unchanged durations.

Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/130316
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/122330


### Changelog category (leave one):
- Performance Improvement


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
A `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` view queried by its own definer is no longer read as an opaque step, so the optimizations of the query apply to it again, as before 26.10 (for example, `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` reads in order through it). Other users, and sessions of the definer that are limited by the `GRANTS` of their authentication method or use other roles, still read such a view sealed, and such sessions of the definer no longer bypass the check that hides its plan in `EXPLAIN`.

### Description

On 26.10, `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` over a `SQL SECURITY DEFINER` view that filters rows reads the whole table: 3,001,000 rows instead of 43,688 in #130316. Since #122330, every `DEFINER` / `NONE` view that can hide rows is read through the opaque `ReadFromSealedView` step, so read-in-order, top-N and the outer predicate for index analysis cannot see through it. The seal keeps hidden rows away from the invoker, but in the report the invoker is the definer.

`StorageView::isReadByDefiner` holds when the query runs with exactly the identity of the view's own query: an initial query of the definer (compared by UUID), with the definer's default roles (current and external), no `GRANTS` limit from the authentication method, and no row policy on the view itself. Such a query can read everything the view hides, so `readImpl` and the `ORDER BY ... LIMIT` pushdown into views no longer seal the view for it. The same check replaces the name-only definer shortcut that decides whether `EXPLAIN` shows the hidden plan. Secondary queries, other users, other role sets and `NONE` views stay sealed. The parallel-replicas carrier, the `Distributed` pushdown and `analyzer_inline_views` keep the structural check.

Reverting #122330 is not proposed: it would reopen the row leak it fixed.

Validation on a debug build: the issue's query reads 43,688 rows as the definer (3,001,000 on master) and still 3,001,000 as another user. The new test fails on master, and each of the six conditions was removed in a separate build, each caught by the test. All 58 tests with `DEFINER` / `NONE` views pass; 05257, 05407 and 05331 now test the sealed path through a non-definer or a `NONE` view. A performance test is added.

issue.body:
At startup, ClickHouse removes `LD_PRELOAD`, `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`, `LD_AUDIT` and similar variables from the environment and re-executes itself. That does not protect against the other ways to inject code into the process. This PR extends the check, `checkHarmfulEnvironment` (formerly `checkHarmfulEnvironmentVariables`), with three more steps that run on Linux with glibc after the environment is clean:

1. **`/etc/ld.so.preload`**: the dynamic loader loads every object listed in this file into every process, the same as with `LD_PRELOAD`, and re-executing does not help. If the file has any entries (comments with `#` are ignored), ClickHouse prints the entries and exits.
2. **Loaded shared objects**: `dl_iterate_phdr` lists everything in the loader's main namespace. Each object must be the main executable, the vDSO, or a transitive `DT_NEEDED` dependency of the executable, matched by `DT_SONAME`. The closure is read from the in-memory dynamic sections, so the allowed set follows from the binary itself (today that's `libc`, `libm`, `libpthread`, `librt`, `libdl` and the loader) and there's no hardcoded per-architecture list. This catches `ld.so --preload` and anything else that slips past the environment check.
3. **Executable file mappings**: auditing libraries (`LD_AUDIT`, `ld.so --audit`) live in a separate loader namespace, which `dl_iterate_phdr` doesn't report. So every file-backed executable mapping in `/proc/self/maps` must belong to the same file (device + inode) as the mapping of one of the expected objects. If `/proc` is not mounted, this step is skipped.

The check runs at the start of `main`, before glibc loads its own plugins on demand (NSS modules, `libgcc_s`).

Tested with a dynamically linked test program built against this file, and with the `clickhouse` binary:
- `server`, `local`, `client` and `keeper` start normally; later on-demand loading by glibc (NSS for name resolution) is not affected;
- plain start, `LD_PRELOAD`/`LD_AUDIT` in the environment (stripped and re-executed as before), and starting through the loader explicitly (`ld.so ./clickhouse`): all start normally;
- `ld.so --preload lib.so`: refused because of the unexpected loaded object;
- `ld.so --audit lib.so`: refused because of the unexpected executable mapping;
- `/etc/ld.so.preload` (tested in a private mount namespace with an overlay on `/etc`): an empty file or one with only comments is accepted, while real or nonexistent entries are refused.

Note: some monitoring agents (e.g. Dynatrace OneAgent) install themselves in `/etc/ld.so.preload`. On such hosts ClickHouse will now refuse to start, so this is marked as a backward-incompatible change.

- Backward Incompatible Change


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
ClickHouse refuses to start if shared objects are injected into its process with `/etc/ld.so.preload`, `ld.so --preload`, or auditing libraries. Previously only the `LD_PRELOAD` and similar environment variables were handled, by removing them and re-executing.

issue.title: Exempt metadata statements from workload scheduling

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Pull request with some product improvements

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Workload scheduler and resource management: CPU/IO/memory scheduling, concurrency control, worklo...

issue.body:
### Changelog category (leave one):
- Improvement

### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Statements that change only metadata, such as `DROP`, `DETACH`, `TRUNCATE`, `RENAME`, `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, `SYSTEM`, `CREATE TABLE` with columns, and `ALTER` that changes the schema, are now exempt from workload scheduling (query-slot and memory-reservation admission, CPU and IO), so they do not queue behind regular queries. The server-wide `max_concurrent_queries*` limits still apply. Previously they were scheduled under the `workload` setting like any other query.

---

Metadata statements share the `workload` setting with regular queries, so under load they queue for query slots, memory reservations, CPU and IO behind data-heavy traffic. This PR exempts them.

`executeQuery` marks a metadata statement on its context (`isMetadataQuery`), and `Context::getWorkloadClassifier` then returns a classifier that maps every resource to an empty `ResourceLink`. The mark is copied to child contexts, so the sub-queries the statement runs are exempt too. `workload` itself is not changed, so the server-wide `max_concurrent_queries*` limits still apply, and sub-queries sent to other servers are scheduled there under `workload`.

`isMetadataQuery` decides by the kind of statement:
- metadata: `DROP` / `DETACH` / `TRUNCATE`, `UNDROP`, `RENAME`, `GRANT`, `REVOKE`, `MOVE` of access entities, `SYSTEM`, `CREATE` / `ATTACH` without a `SELECT` or a table function, and `ALTER` without commands that copy parts in the query (`MOVE`, `REPLACE`, `FETCH`, `ATTACH`, `FREEZE` partition, `EXECUTE`);
- everything else, e.g. `CREATE ... AS SELECT`, views, `OPTIMIZE`, `BACKUP`, `RESTORE`, stays under `workload`.

The classification is best effort: a metadata statement can still do data work that its text does not show (e.g. a target engine that loads or flushes data, or a stored expression with a subquery). A metadata statement wrapped by `EXECUTE AS` or `PARALLEL WITH` runs as an internal query; its CPU and IO follow the wrapping statement's `workload`.

issue.title: Iceberg: CREATE TABLE ... ORDER BY writes null-order nulls-first, but ClickHouse sorts NULLs last

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: To be reviewed by developers and confirmed/rejected.

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Data lake table formats (Iceberg/Delta/Hudi) integration.

issue.body:
### Company or project name

ClickHouse

### Describe what's wrong

`CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = Iceberg... ORDER BY x` writes the sort order with `"null-order": "nulls-first"` (hardcoded in `src/Storages/ObjectStorage/DataLakes/Iceberg/Utils.cpp`), while ClickHouse sorts rows by that key with NULLs last for `ASC` (`sortBlockByKeyDescription`, nulls direction 1).

The table metadata therefore describes a different order than the one ClickHouse writes. Data files written by ClickHouse are not tagged with `sort_order_id` today, so nothing relies on it yet, but:
- another engine writing sorted files to this table follows `nulls-first`, while ClickHouse's in-order read assumes NULLs last for the same key (not checked);
- tagging ClickHouse-written files as sorted would claim an order they do not have.

### Does it reproduce on the most recent release?

Reproduced on master (`6e962c3b7e0`, 26.11). Not checked on a release.

### How to reproduce

```sql
CREATE TABLE t (x Nullable(Int64)) ENGINE = IcebergLocal('/path/t') ORDER BY x;
INSERT INTO t SELECT if(number % 3 = 0, NULL, number) FROM numbers(9) SETTINGS max_threads = 1, max_insert_threads = 1;
SELECT x FROM file('/path/t/data/*.parquet', Parquet);
```

- Stored rows: `1, 2, 4, 5, 7, 8, NULL, NULL, NULL` (NULLs last).
- `metadata/v2.metadata.json`: `"sort-orders": [{"fields": [{"direction": "asc", "null-order": "nulls-first", "source-id": 1, "transform": "identity"}], "order-id": 1}]`.

### Expected behavior

The written `null-order` matches what ClickHouse sorts: `nulls-last` for `ASC`, `nulls-first` for `DESC` (or the sort follows the declared `null-order`).

### Error message and/or stacktrace

None.

comment.body:
I opened #130628: `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = Iceberg... ORDER BY` now declares `nulls-last` for an ascending field and `nulls-first` for a descending one, the placement ClickHouse sorts by and assumes in read in order. With the old `nulls-first`, on 26.10 `SELECT ... ORDER BY x` returns the NULLs first after Spark writes sorted files to such a table.

Tables that already declare `asc nulls-first` (Spark's default) are still read with ClickHouse's placement; that is #126653. Your draft #130579 expects `nulls-first` in its `nullable` case, so whichever of the two merges second updates that expectation.

### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Fix `SELECT ... ORDER BY` returning NULLs first on an Iceberg table that ClickHouse created with `ORDER BY` on a `Nullable` column, after another engine such as Spark wrote sorted files to it. `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = Iceberg... ORDER BY` now declares `null-order` `nulls-last` for an ascending field, the order ClickHouse sorts by, instead of `nulls-first` for every field. Closes #130441.

### Description

On 26.10, when Spark writes to an Iceberg table that ClickHouse created with `ORDER BY x` on a `Nullable` column, `SELECT x FROM t ORDER BY x` returns the NULLs first, because the table declares `nulls-first` while ClickHouse reads it as NULLs last (measured on `26.10.2.103` and master: `\N \N 1 2 3`; with `optimize_read_in_order = 0`, `1 2 3 \N \N`).

`createEmptyMetadataFile` wrote `"null-order": "nulls-first"` for every sort field. ClickHouse has one NULL placement for a sorting key: NULLs compare greater than any value, so they come last for an ascending key and first for a descending one. `INSERT` sorts an Iceberg table that way (`sortBlockByKeyDescription`) and read in order assumes it. Spark follows the declaration, so its files had NULLs first under a `sort_order_id` that ClickHouse trusts, and the sort was dropped.

Now an ascending field declares `nulls-last` and a descending one `nulls-first`. Only newly created tables change; both values are valid Iceberg and nothing in ClickHouse reads `null-order` back. Tables that declare the opposite placement (Spark's default `asc nulls-first`) are still read with ClickHouse's placement: that is #126653. Releases before 26.10 write sort order id 0, which Spark refuses, so they are not affected this way.

Draft #130579 makes `INSERT` follow the declared `null-order`; its `nullable` case expects today's `nulls-first`, so whichever of the two merges second updates that expectation.

Validation: `05618_iceberg_sort_order_null_order` checks the declared order and the order `INSERT` writes, for `ASC` and `DESC`. It fails on master (`[('asc','nulls-first')]`) and passes 50/50 with randomized settings. A local Spark run (not committed) gives the wrong `ORDER BY` result, and the correct one with the fix.

Looks good to me. I built `d40f83a7` and the same tree without the `applyParallelReplicas.cpp` hunk, and compared them on a three-replica localhost cluster.

### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Install `pigz` in the `clickhouse/binary-builder` image, so the release build jobs compress their `.tgz` packages in parallel.

### Description

`packages/build` already compresses the `.tgz` tarballs with `pigz` when `/usr/bin/pigz` exists, else with `tar -czf`. The `Build Packages` step of `Build (amd_release)` / `Build (arm_release)` runs inside `clickhouse/binary-builder`, which does not install `pigz` (checked in the current master image `16143eb26bdf0bdb2f00_amd`), so every tarball is compressed by single-threaded `gzip`. The four tarballs took 60 s of the 69 s step in [a PR `arm_release` job](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/42315009375/job/128354633601), and 248 s of 282 s in a [master `amd_release` job](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/actions/runs/42598309267).

This PR adds `pigz` to the image's package list. Nothing else changes. This PR's own `Build (amd_release)` / `Build (arm_release)` do not exercise it: they are reused from the CI cache, because the build-job digests do not include the `binary-builder` image digest (`ci/praktika/digest.py`).

Validation, locally on the master `26.11.1.1733` packages with the same `pigz` 2.8, `gzip` 1.12 and GNU tar 1.35 as the image, median of 3 runs on 16 cores:
- `clickhouse-common-static` (746 MB): `gzip` 25.0 s, `pigz` 2.1 s (1.4 s on 32 cores, the size of the `m8g.8xlarge` runner).
- `clickhouse-common-static-dbg` (4.1 GB): `gzip` 117.8 s, `pigz` 12.7 s (7.2 s on 32 cores).

The decompressed tar streams are byte-identical to `gzip`'s, `sha512sum -c` passes, and BusyBox `tar xzf` in Alpine (the path of the Alpine server and keeper images) extracts the same files. issue.title: Iceberg: ORDER BY ... DESC returns ascending rows on a table sorted ASC (read-in-order)

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: To be reviewed by developers and confirmed/rejected.

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Data lake table formats (Iceberg/Delta/Hudi) integration.

issue.body:
### Company or project name

ClickHouse

### Describe what's wrong

For an Iceberg table sorted `ASC` whose data files all carry the table's `sort_order_id`, `ORDER BY x DESC LIMIT n` returns the smallest values in ascending order. `buildInputOrderInfo` (`optimizeReadInOrder.cpp`) accepts an input order with `direction = -1` for `ReadFromObjectStorageStep`, but the files are only ever read forwards.

### Does it reproduce on the most recent release?

Reproduced on master (`6e962c3b7e0`, 26.11). Not checked on a release.

### How to reproduce

The table needs data files tagged with `sort_order_id` (e.g. written by Spark with a table sort order). I wrote it with a local ClickHouse build that tags inserted files and read it with a master build:

```sql
-- written with a build that tags files: 1 data file, sort_order_id = 1
CREATE TABLE t (x Int64) ENGINE = IcebergLocal('/path/t') ORDER BY x;
INSERT INTO t SELECT number FROM numbers(1000);

-- read with master
SELECT x FROM icebergLocal('/path/t') ORDER BY x DESC LIMIT 5;
```

Result: `0 1 2 3 4`. With `optimize_read_in_order = 0`: `999 998 997 996 995`.

### Expected behavior

`999 998 997 996 995`. Either read the files in reverse, or do not read in order when the requested direction differs from the table's sort order.

### Error message and/or stacktrace

None; the result is silently wrong.

comment.body:
This is fixed by #113095 (mine, open), the second option you list: `ReadFromObjectStorageStep::requestReadingInOrder` declines any direction other than ascending, since there is no reverse file walk, so the sorting step is kept. Its `test_read_in_order` asserts that `ORDER BY id DESC` returns `4, 3, 2, 1` with `PartialSortingTransform` still in the pipeline, and it passed in CI at the PR head (7f67ed3).

The PR has merge conflicts with master now; I'll resolve them and link this issue from its description.

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca

issue.body:
<!--
Linked issues and pull requests. Use full GitHub URLs, one relationship per line; delete the lines you don't need.

Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN   (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch)
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN
-->

Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/130416
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/130231


### Changelog category (leave one):
- Performance Improvement


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Writing Iceberg metadata files with `iceberg_metadata_compression_method = 'zstd'` now sizes the zstd context to the file instead of to the compression level: at `output_format_compression_level = 22` the memory of an `INSERT` or `CREATE TABLE` drops from about 836 MiB to about 1.5 MiB.

### Description

Every `.metadata.json` written with zstd (each `CREATE TABLE` and each commit) allocated a context sized for the level, not for the file: ~836 MiB at level 22 for a few hundred bytes, allocated by libzstd and so not checked against `max_memory_usage` (#130416).

`Iceberg::writeMessageToFile` has the whole message in memory but streamed it through `ZstdDeflatingWriteBuffer`, whose `finalize` sends `ZSTD_e_flush` before `ZSTD_e_end`. zstd infers the source size only when the first call of a frame is `ZSTD_e_end`, so it kept the level's full parameters. The fix compresses the message with one `ZSTD_compress2` call (same level, same checksum flag), the same approach #130231 takes for Parquet pages. Doing it in the caller also covers metadata larger than the 1 MiB buffer, where a size pledge at `finalize` would not help. Other codecs are unchanged.

Measured on a debug build (`system.query_log.memory_usage`, CREATE / INSERT of the issue's repro): level 22 835.7 / 835.8 MiB -> 1.3 / 1.5 MiB, level 19 91.6 / 91.8 MiB -> 1.3 / 1.5 MiB, level 3 5.6 / 5.7 MiB -> 1.1 / 1.3 MiB. For a 2.9 MB metadata file the CREATE drops from 857 MiB to 91 MiB at level 22 and is unchanged (28.6 MiB) at level 3. The new frames also record the content size; old and new versions read and extend each other's tables.

The Iceberg REST catalog server writes metadata only as `none` or `gzip`, so its writer is not affected. `xz` at level 9 still uses ~675 MiB (its preset dictionary, a different mechanism), unchanged here.

The new test fails on master (`memory_usage` above 500 MB) and passes with the fix.

issue.body:
Replaces the C++ `DWARF` input format parser (`DWARFBlockInputFormat`, `DB::Elf`, `llvm::DWARFContext`) with a Rust crate in `contrib/dwarf-cmake` (`ch_rust::dwarf`) built on the already-vendored `gimli 0.33.0`, `object 0.39.1`, and `memchr 2.8.3` crates (no `contrib/rust_vendor` changes).

`DWARFBlockInputFormat` keeps ownership of the `MMappedFile` / `PODArray<char>` input buffer and the worker queue. Rust parses the ELF64 header, debug sections, compilation units, DIEs, line tables, and range lists (`#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in all parser modules, `unsafe` only in `ffi.rs` with `catch_unwind`), and writes batches directly into ClickHouse `PODArray` column buffers via reserve/cancel callbacks. `ENABLE_DWARF_PARSER` is also decoupled from `contrib/llvm-project-cmake`, so enabling `DWARF` alone no longer builds or links `LLVMDebugInfoDWARF`.

30-run ABBA results on `c7i.4xlarge` (5.09 GB `clickhouse` binary, 140.2M rows, `FORMAT Null`):
```text
SELECT ranges (t=8):                    7.58s -> 6.10s (0.81x time, 0.60x instructions)
SELECT offset (t=1 / t=2 / t=8):       36.42s -> 28.00s / 17.30s -> 13.25s / 7.24s -> 6.05s (0.77x-0.83x time, 0.61x instructions)
SELECT tag, ancestor_* (t=8):           7.86s -> 6.58s (0.84x time, 0.74x instructions)
SELECT name, linkage_name, decl_* (t=8):7.56s -> 6.40s (0.85x time, 0.71x instructions)
SELECT attr_* (t=8):                    8.70s -> 7.75s (0.89x time, 0.86x instructions)
SELECT * (t=8 / t=16):                 10.79s -> 10.06s / 11.07s -> 10.38s (0.93x-0.94x time, 0.99x instructions)
Stripped binary / .text delta:         -363.6 KiB / -380.1 KiB
```

Valid fixture outputs match the old parser bit-for-bit across the 85-file differential corpus (`02225`, `02896`, `04340`, `05139`, `05507` pass; 89 Rust tests pass under Miri, ASan, and TSan; 23.2M ASan libFuzzer runs on `format_fuzzer` and `dwarf_abi_fuzzer` with 0 crashes). Intentional rejections of malformed/non-ELF64-LE inputs that the old parser accepted or truncated (such as `E-02`/`E-03`/`E-06`/`E-11`, `U-01`/`U-07`/`U-08`/`U-10`/`U-15`/`U-16`, `F-16`, and `L-03`/`L-05`) are documented in `contrib/dwarf-cmake/COMPATIBILITY.md`.

Two things to confirm with maintainers:
- Preliminary cross-targets with `ENABLE_RUST=OFF` (`riscv64`, `loongarch64`, `illumos`) have `USE_DWARF_PARSER` off (`s390x`, `ppc64le`, `x86_64`, and `aarch64` build with `ENABLE_RUST=ON`).
- Malformed unit headers (including raw `SHF_COMPRESSED` `.debug_info` where the old parser logged a stderr warning and returned 0 rows) and the other tightened cases in `COMPATIBILITY.md` now return `CANNOT_PARSE_ELF` or `CANNOT_PARSE_DWARF`.

### Changelog category (leave one):
- Improvement

### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Replace the `DWARF` input format parser (`DWARFBlockInputFormat`) with a Rust implementation (`contrib/dwarf-cmake`) using `gimli` and `object`.

Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN   (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch)

### Changelog category (leave one):
- Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Fixed filters on `toString` of an integer key, such as `toString(key) = '999999999999999999'`, skipping matching rows when one granule (or one `minmax` skip index granule) held integers of 15 or more digits with different numbers of digits. `toString(key) IN (subquery)` (also `CAST(key AS String)`) over an integer or `Date` key uses the primary key again when the subquery returns integers (or dates), as before 26.10. Closes #130315.

### Description

Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/130315
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/118957

On 26.3, 26.8 and 26.10, `toString(k) = '999999999999999999'` over a `UInt64` key returns 0 instead of 1 when one granule holds 999999999999999999 and 1000000000000000000. `ToStringMonotonicity` compared `floor(log10(x))` in `double`, which gives `n` for `x = 10^n - 1` from 15 digits on, so such a range counted as monotonic although its texts are in the opposite order. The digit count is now exact (`common::digits10`); 0 stays apart from 1..9 as before, because a `Bool` renders them as configurable strings.

Since #118957 (26.10), `toString(k) IN (SELECT <integers>)` over an integer sorting key reads every granule, where 26.8 pruned (#130315). #118957 declines a non-`String` set element over a string column, because `IN` parses the column (`'02'` and `'2'` are both `2`) while the index renders the element. When the string is the text that the key's own chain computes from a native integer (`toString`, `CAST`/`_CAST` to `String`), it holds only canonical numerals, so the set and the index agree; the same holds for `Date`. The decline now exempts exactly that case; types with a custom serialization (`Bool`, also inside `SimpleAggregateFunction`) stay declined. This path needs the exact digit count: 26.8 pruned it with the same wrong result. Reverting #118957 would bring back the wrong results it fixed (`s IN (SELECT toUInt8(2))` over a `String` key holding `'02'`).

Validation: on the issue's setup the first parent of #118957 and this PR select 1186/3668 granules, master 3668/3668, 39 rows on all. Both tests fail on master; every indexed count matches a full-scan `countIf`, and `max_rows_to_read` checks pin the pruning, also for 19-digit keys. 50 randomized runs pass.

Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN
-->
Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/130317
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/117248


### Changelog category (leave one):
- Performance Improvement


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
A `FINAL` query on a table whose row policy compares `ORDER BY` columns with a value computed once per query, such as `currentUser()`, `now()` or an `IN (subquery)` set, applies the policy before the merge again, as in 26.8, instead of reading and merging every row first. Closes #130317.

### Description

Since 26.9 a row policy like `c2 = substring(currentUser(), 1, 3)` on an `ORDER BY` column is applied after `FINAL`, and PREWHERE with it, so the whole table is read and merged before the policy filters it. On the query in #130317 this costs 9.7x memory and 2.7x time with the same result. Policies using `now()`, `currentDatabase()` or `IN (subquery)` are deferred too.

#117248 added `node->isDeterministic()` to `isNodeDeterministic`, the gate of `isRowPolicyDeferredAfterFinal`. For a `COLUMN` node it returns `is_deterministic_constant`, which the analyzer sets to false for a constant folded from a non-deterministic function. Applying the policy before `FINAL` only needs every version of one key to get the same verdict, and a constant has one value for the whole query, so it cannot split a dedup group. Only a lambda folded into a constant is evaluated per row, and `allNodeFunctions` still checks its body, so the cases #117248 fixed stay deferred (05141, 05182). This PR removes that check; the flag itself stays, the query condition cache needs it. I do not propose reverting #117248: it fixes wrong results (#117016).

On a `GraphiteMergeTree` table such a policy is again applied before the rollup, as a literal policy already is (26.8 behaviour, see #112817).

Validation: new test `05616_row_policy_after_final_query_constant` fails on master (the policy is deferred) and passes 50/50 with random settings, in the parallel-replicas flavour and with `serialize_query_plan = 1`. New performance test `final_row_policy_query_constant`. On the master release build, the issue's data, the `currentUser()` policy (the plan master uses) against the same policy as a literal (the plan this PR restores): 0.093 s / 1.20 GiB against 0.029 s / 288 MiB, and 0.183 s / 3.47 GiB against 0.033 s / 453 MiB with `compatibility = '24.0'` (medians of 10).

issue.title: Reduce memory usage of writing zstd Iceberg metadata at high compression levels

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca

issue.body:
<!--

Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/NNNNN   (auto-closes the issue when this PR is merged into the default branch)
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/NNNNN
-->

Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/130416
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/130231


### Changelog category (leave one):
- Performance Improvement


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Writing Iceberg metadata files with `iceberg_metadata_compression_method = 'zstd'` now sizes the zstd context to the file instead of to the compression level: at `output_format_compression_level = 22` the memory of an `INSERT` or `CREATE TABLE` drops from about 836 MiB to about 1.5 MiB.

### Description

Every `.metadata.json` written with zstd (each `CREATE TABLE` and each commit) allocated a context sized for the level, not for the file: ~836 MiB at level 22 for a few hundred bytes, allocated by libzstd and so not checked against `max_memory_usage` (#130416).

`Iceberg::writeMessageToFile` has the whole message in memory but streamed it through `ZstdDeflatingWriteBuffer`, whose `finalize` sends `ZSTD_e_flush` before `ZSTD_e_end`. zstd infers the source size only when the first call of a frame is `ZSTD_e_end`, so it kept the level's full parameters. The fix compresses the message with one `ZSTD_compress2` call (same level, same checksum flag), the same approach #130231 takes for Parquet pages. Doing it in the caller also covers metadata larger than the 1 MiB buffer, where a size pledge at `finalize` would not help. Other codecs are unchanged.

Measured on a debug build (`system.query_log.memory_usage`, CREATE / INSERT of the issue's repro): level 22 835.7 / 835.8 MiB -> 1.3 / 1.5 MiB, level 19 91.6 / 91.8 MiB -> 1.3 / 1.5 MiB, level 3 5.6 / 5.7 MiB -> 1.1 / 1.3 MiB. For a 2.9 MB metadata file the CREATE drops from 857 MiB to 91 MiB at level 22 and is unchanged (28.6 MiB) at level 3. The new frames also record the content size; old and new versions read and extend each other's tables.

The Iceberg REST catalog server writes metadata only as `none` or `gzip`, so its writer is not affected. `xz` at level 9 still uses ~675 MiB (its preset dictionary, a different mechanism), unchanged here.

The new test fails on master (`memory_usage` above 500 MB) and passes with the fix.

issue.title: Fix RabbitMQ engine stopping consumption when the backlog exceeds the internal queue

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Pull request with bugfix, not backported by default

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Message queue integrations (Kafka, RabbitMQ, NATS table engines for stream ingestion/egress).

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Allows running workflows for external contributors

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Author is not a member of the ClickHouse organization

issue.body:
Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/54775
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/74430
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/50692
Depends on: https://github.com/ClickHouse/AMQP-CPP/pull/9 and the submodule bump that follows it (see "Dependency" below)

### Changelog category (leave one):
- Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)

### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Fixes `RabbitMQ` tables that silently stop consuming, with `DROP TABLE` hanging until a restart, when inserts fall far behind the broker (about 1 million messages with default settings, 100000 with a small `rabbitmq_max_block_size`). ClickHouse now limits how many unacknowledged messages RabbitMQ sends at once.

### Description
The consumer sets no `basic.qos`, so RabbitMQ pushes every ready message into a bounded queue of `max(100000, block size)` entries (block size: `rabbitmq_max_block_size`, or `max_insert_block_size / rabbitmq_num_consumers` = 1048449 by default). Once inserts are that far behind, the libuv delivery callback blocks in `push()` while `streamToViews`, the only thread that drains the queue, waits for the loop task to return: consumption stops without any error in the log and `DROP TABLE` hangs in `shutdown()`. In production this hits as soon as inserts fall behind under load: consumption stops without any error, `DROP TABLE` hangs, and only a server restart recovers. Because of this we had to build our own ingestion system instead of using the RabbitMQ engine.

Fix:
1. Non-global `basic.qos` per subscription, `clamp(queue_size / num_queues, 1, 65535)` (65535 unless there are several queues). A channel then has at most `num_queues * prefetch_count <= queue_size` deliveries outstanding, so `received` never fills and the delivery callback never waits for space.
2. Ack messages that produce no rows, so they cannot hold prefetch slots forever.
3. End a block once the channel's prefetch window is used up and nothing is pending, instead of waiting for the flush interval. The window counts messages an earlier reader of the pooled consumer left unacked (a direct `SELECT`); if they hold all of it, the block acks them, as the next block does on master.

**Dependency.** With the AMQP-CPP currently pinned, one `basic.nack` (a failed insert into a view, `SYSTEM STOP/CANCEL` during a block) makes AMQP-CPP queue every later ack without sending it (#76163). On master that gives duplicates; with a prefetch window the broker stops after 65535 unacked messages and the table stalls until it reconnects. Measured: one failing message, then 70000 messages:

| binary | AMQP-CPP | consumed |
|---|---|---|
| master | 4fccd7f (pin) | 70000 of 70000 |
| this PR | 4fccd7f (pin) | stops at 65535 (broker: 65535 unacked, 0 acks) |
| this PR | c0049e0 (AMQP-CPP#9) | 70000 of 70000 |

So this PR should merge after AMQP-CPP#9 and its submodule bump.

Behaviour changes:
- A block ends after at most `prefetch_count` messages per consumer (65535, or `queue_size / num_queues` with several queues, documented), so a large `rabbitmq_max_block_size` can give more, smaller parts. Draining a 300000-message backlog with default settings takes the same time as on master (8.5–8.9 s vs 8.8–8.9 s, 7 parts each, 3 runs each).
- A direct `SELECT` without `rabbitmq_commit_on_select` still leaves what it read unacked, as on master, and a view's next block acks it. Without a view, `prefetch_count` (up to 65535) such reads use up the window until the connection is re-established.
- The window makes a pre-existing lost wake-up in `waitForMessages` likelier: with `rabbitmq_flush_interval_ms = 0` a block can sleep until the next delivery or the sanity timeout. Fixed in a follow-up PR.

Tests: five new integration tests pass with the fix at `3a227d8e483` (3 of 3 runs each after merging master with #125105, 10 of 10 before). Four fail on current master; the fifth, a window held entirely by direct `SELECT`s, fails on `ed652fa8d` and passes on master, which has no window. Before the merge, the rest of `test_storage_rabbitmq` passed on a minimal local build, except two tests that need Arrow or the JSON type and failed on master too.

Repro, one minute on the official 26.9 image: https://gist.github.com/comino/349122b3f425d277569c08187289852f

<details><summary>Stacks and design notes</summary>

Stacks while stuck (`system.stack_trace`, official 26.9.12.8, shortened):
```
loop thread:      pthread_cond_wait <- RabbitMQConsumer::subscribe()::$_1 <- … <- AMQP::DeferredReceiver::process <- uv_run <- RabbitMQHandler::startLoop
streaming thread: mutex::lock <- BackgroundSchedulePoolTaskInfo::deactivate <- StorageRabbitMQ::streamToViews
DROP TABLE:       mutex::lock <- StorageRabbitMQ::shutdown <- InterpreterDropQuery::executeToTableImpl
```

- QoS is non-global because global QoS is deprecated and rejected by quorum and stream queues.
- No new settings and no queue or exchange declaration changes, so existing tables and queues keep working.
- Side effect: without `basic.qos`, RabbitMQ caps quorum-queue consumers at 2000 unacked messages; with an explicit prefetch a 20000-message quorum backlog drained in 8 s instead of 56 s (RabbitMQ 4, `rabbitmq_flush_interval_ms = 5000`).
- Tests: `test_rabbitmq_backlog_larger_than_received_queue`, `test_rabbitmq_empty_messages_are_acked` (waits for the ack in the log), `test_rabbitmq_block_ends_when_prefetch_is_used_up`, `test_rabbitmq_view_acks_messages_a_select_left_unacked`, `test_rabbitmq_view_acks_a_window_selects_left_unacked`.
</details>

cc @alexey-milovidov

issue.title: Faster builds: no-op rebuild 21 s → 1.4 s, header edits up to −72%, clean build −21% (10 build-system, include and PCH patches)

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Build system (CMake, compilation, platform builds).

issue.body:
### Describe the situation

Small edits rebuild far more than they need: each ClickHouse build reruns cargo and rewrites the Rust archives, so clickhouse relinks, and settings files and core headers pull thousands of files into the rebuild. These patches remove most of that work; precompiled headers speed up clean builds.

<details><summary>What each patch changes, per-patch measurements and checks</summary>

1. **Link fix.** In our default RelWithDebInfo builds with clang/lld 21.1.8, master's `clickhouse` failed to link: `localize_rust_c_symbols.sh` rewrites the Rust archives with `llvm-objcopy` (`llvm-objcopy-21`, the `CMAKE_OBJCOPY` of these builds), which leaves `.llvm_addrsig` sections with `sh_link=0` in the objects where it localizes a symbol; lld's `--icf=safe` warns about them and `--fatal-warnings` fails the link. #126478 alone does not fix these builds: it makes CMake pass the LLVM objcopy instead of GNU objcopy, and these builds already used it. With `-Wl,--no-fatal-warnings` in the linker flags the link succeeds; we did not try CI's toolchain. The patch removes `.llvm_addrsig` there, as `strip_rust_symbols.sh` does since #122904; this works with GNU objcopy too. Patch 1 is a link fix that both measured trees contain; it is not measured on its own.
2. **Build system and settings.** Today every build runs the cargo builds and rewrites the copied Rust archives in place (`localize_rust_c_symbols.sh`, `strip_rust_symbols.sh`), so the copy never matches cargo's output, is rewritten again and `clickhouse` relinks even when nothing changed; every library linking a crate also waits for all cargo builds before compiling anything. The patch (a) runs each post-processing step as a custom command that writes a new archive only when its input changed (the approach of #119121); (b) builds the workspace crates with one `cargo build`, so they no longer wait for each other on cargo's target-directory lock, and skips cargo when no input of the Rust libraries changed (`cmake/cargo_if_changed.sh`, which checks cargo's dep-info files and falls back to running cargo); (c) links the crates through imported targets without the cargo dependency, so C++ compiles run in parallel with cargo and only the sources including `delta_kernel_ffi.hpp` wait for the delta-kernel build; (d) on a CMake re-run, rewrites configure-time generated files only when their content changes, lists licenses without a fork per vendored crate and keeps `git status` out of submodule work trees; (e) for the settings files, replaces per-setting template code with table-driven accessors in `BaseSettings.h` and shared field operations, includes `FormatFactorySettings.h` only where it is used and moves the disk checks of `MergeTreeSettings.cpp` to `MergeTreeSettingsDisks.cpp` (no more `MergeTreeData.h`, `ZooKeeper.h`, `ASTFunction.h`). Measured separately on x86, part (a) alone took the no-op rebuild from 21.1 to 4.4 s and the rest of the build-system changes to 1.3 s; part (e) alone took a `Settings.cpp` edit from 42.8 to 28.2 s. One `cargo build` for all workspace crates unifies the features of the dependencies they share, as `cargo build --workspace` does, so the linked Rust code changes slightly: on an earlier master this change alone made the binary 0.3 MB smaller, while the 136 exported Rust FFI symbols and the outputs of PRQL, polyglot, PCO and Vortex smoke queries stayed identical; skim and wasmtime were linked but not run.
3. **ProtocolDefines.h and friends.** The parallel-replicas protocol versions move to `ParallelReplicasProtocolDefines.h`, so `RequestResponse.h` (and everything including it) no longer depends on `ProtocolDefines.h`; `FileCachePolicy` moves to `Core/FileCachePolicy.h`, so `FileCache_fwd.h` no longer includes `SettingsEnums.h`; `ActionsDAG.h` and `IQueryPlanStep.h` are replaced by forward declarations where one suffices. A `ProtocolDefines.h` edit recompiles 115 files instead of 278.
4. **Direct includes.** 87 files that used `FormatSettings` (and a few other headers) through transitive includes include them directly. Patch 4 only adds the direct includes that patch 5 needs; it is not measured on its own.
5. **FormatSettings.h out of common headers.** `ReadHelpers.h`, `WriteHelpers.h`, `FormatFactorySettings.h`, `SettingsEnums.h` and `Context.h` included the whole `FormatSettings.h`. The CSV/JSON enums they need move to `FormatSettingsEnums.h` and the JSON number writers to `writeJSONNumber.h`/`WriteHelpers.cpp`: a `FormatSettings.h` edit recompiles 1,203 files instead of 3,222.
6. **FormatSettings.h out of the remaining wide headers.** `NativeWriter.h`, `DateTimeTransforms.h`, `FunctionBinaryArithmetic.h`, `convertFieldToType.h`, `convertColumnToType.h`, `VirtualColumnUtils.h` and a few others stop including it: 708 files instead of 1,203.
7. **Operators.h and IDataType.h.** `IO/Operators.h` no longer includes `IO/ReadHelpers.h` (a `ReadHelpers.h` edit: 1,338 files instead of 2,002, 1,147 → 933 s (−19%) when measured alone), and `IDataType.h` no longer includes `ISerialization.h`; the substream types it needs move to `SerializationSubstream.h` (an `ISerialization.h` edit: 2,286 files instead of 3,218, 1,516 → 1,267 s (−16%) alone).
8. **Unit-test include.** One unit test used `ISerialization.h` through `IDataType.h`. Patch 8 only adds an include to one unit test; it is not measured on its own.
9. **Precompiled headers.** `cmake/precompiled_headers.cmake` adds per-target PCHs of stable standard-library, fmt, magic_enum, `base/` and third-party headers to the 15 largest `src` targets and the largest contrib libraries, with `-fno-pch-timestamp` so ccache still hits in a new build directory. Earlier attempts found little gain: #9162 (2020) measured a clean build of 74 minutes with PCH against 76 without, and the `dbms`-only PCH listed in #96721 saved 5.9 s, about 3% of CPU time, at 192 cores. Patch 9 covers far more of the build, including the contrib sources that mostly parse their library headers: on these 16-core hosts it cut clean-build CPU time by 19% (x86) and 18% (ARM) and wall time by 18.8% and 17.5%, with the same `.text` size. Compiler caches stay correct: after a change of only the PCH content, sccache 0.19, chcache and ccache 4.9.1 all missed, because the headers inside the PCH are part of what each cache hashes; ccache gets the `pch_defines,time_macros` sloppiness it needs only for the targets with a PCH. We did not measure CI builds with sccache, where every fresh build directory builds the PCHs again.
10. **Opt-in SPLIT_DWARF.** A `SPLIT_DWARF` CMake option (`-gsplit-dwarf -gno-gnu-pubnames`) keeps most debug information out of the objects the linker reads. `Dwarf.cpp` accepts the skeleton units (`DW_TAG_skeleton_unit`) so stack traces keep file and line, and one test that reads the binary's DWARF is skipped in split builds, as it is for `-g0`.

### How to reproduce

<details><summary>Hosts, configuration and measurement procedure</summary>

- Hosts: x86, AWS r6i.8xlarge (16 cores / 32 vCPU, 247 GiB); ARM, AWS r7g.4xlarge (16 vCPU Graviton3, 123 GiB); Ubuntu 24.04.
- Toolchain: clang/lld 21.1.8 from apt.llvm.org, CMake 3.28.3, Ninja 1.11.1, ccache 4.9.1, Rust nightly-2026-03-22 as pinned by `contrib/corrosion-cmake`.
- Configuration (both arms): `cmake -S . -B build -G Ninja -DCMAKE_C_COMPILER=clang-21 -DCMAKE_CXX_COMPILER=clang++-21`, then `ninja -C build clickhouse` (default parallelism, ccache through `COMPILER_CACHE=auto`). Patch 10 is measured with `-DSPLIT_DWARF=ON` against the same tree without it.
- Trees: one source checkout and one `CCACHE_DIR` per arm, never shared. Before each incremental run the tree is synced with two no-op `ninja` runs.
- Scenarios, each timed from the edit to the finished `clickhouse` binary:
  - no-op: `ninja` on the synced tree;
  - leaf, `Settings.cpp`, `ServerSettings.cpp`, `MergeTreeSettings.cpp` and header edits: append a unique comment line to the file, `ninja`, then restore the file (the next sync rebuilds it);
  - CMake re-run: `touch CMakeLists.txt`, `ninja`;
  - new build directory with warm ccache: delete the build directory, `cmake` + `ninja`;
  - clean build: delete the build directory and the arm's ccache directory, `cmake` + `ninja`.
- Order: arms interleaved per scenario (A,B,B,A or A,B,B,A,A,B), 2 pairs for scenarios over 5 minutes, 3 for the others; the table shows medians and the 95% interval of the paired geometric ratio. The arm for patch 9 alone (all patches except 9 vs all patches) was interleaved with the same runs on x86.
- Patch application: 1 → 9 in order on master 64576f956c6b; patch 10 applies on top.

</details>

### Expected performance

<details><summary>Expected behavior</summary>

A rebuild should cost about as much as the change: no cargo run, archive rewrite or relink when no Rust input and no object changed; after a header edit, recompiling only the files that use the header; after a CMake re-run with no real change, no regenerated file that forces recompiles. Clean builds should not parse the same large third-party headers in every translation unit.

</details>

**Patch 1: link fix for the localized Rust archives**

```diff
diff --git a/cmake/localize_rust_c_symbols.sh b/cmake/localize_rust_c_symbols.sh
index 61cf95aa9c8..4ef48524c02 100755
--- a/cmake/localize_rust_c_symbols.sh
+++ b/cmake/localize_rust_c_symbols.sh
@@ -125,12 +125,15 @@ if [ -s "$LOCALIZE_FILE" ]; then
     # Some Rust archives contain non-ELF members (e.g. debug metadata objects)
     # that cause llvm-objcopy to fail.  In that case, fall back to extracting
     # individual members, processing only valid ELF objects, and repacking.
-    if ! "$OBJCOPY" --localize-symbols="$LOCALIZE_FILE" "$LIB_PATH" 2>/dev/null; then
+    # Also drop .llvm_addrsig: objcopy leaves its sh_link at 0, and lld --icf=safe then warns that it ignores it
+    # (an error with --fatal-warnings). Without the table lld treats these objects conservatively, as it does
+    # when it ignores the table. See strip_rust_symbols.sh.
+    if ! "$OBJCOPY" --localize-symbols="$LOCALIZE_FILE" --remove-section=.llvm_addrsig "$LIB_PATH" 2>/dev/null; then
         WORK_DIR=$(mktemp -d)
 
         (cd "$WORK_DIR" && "$AR" x "$LIB_PATH")
         for obj in "$WORK_DIR"/*.o; do
-            "$OBJCOPY" --localize-symbols="$LOCALIZE_FILE" "$obj" 2>/dev/null || true
+            "$OBJCOPY" --localize-symbols="$LOCALIZE_FILE" --remove-section=.llvm_addrsig "$obj" 2>/dev/null || true
         done
         "$AR" rcs "$LIB_PATH" "$WORK_DIR"/*.o
     fi
```

```diff
+# Precompiled headers of stable third-party headers.
+#
+# Most of the compile time of a typical ClickHouse source file is spent in the frontend, re-parsing the same
+# standard library headers for every translation unit. The headers below are used by most sources and change
+# only with toolchain or contrib updates, apart from a few base/ headers that almost every source includes anyway.
+# Each target builds its own PCH with its own flags. Sources with their own compile flags (-march, -O3,
+# -U_LIBCPP_HARDENING_MODE, ...) cannot use that PCH and are compiled as before.
+#
+# The largest contrib libraries get a PCH of their own public headers as well: their sources are small and
+# spend most of their compile time parsing the library headers, which change only with the submodule.
+#
+# Compiler caches: sccache and chcache hash the preprocessed source, which includes the PCH headers.
+# ccache refuses PCH compiles unless its sloppiness includes pch_defines,time_macros, so it is added
+# to the launcher of the targets that use the PCH (ClickHouse sources do not use __DATE__ or __TIME__).
+
+option (ENABLE_PRECOMPILED_HEADERS "Precompile common standard library, fmt and magic_enum headers for the largest targets" ON)
+option (ENABLE_CONTRIB_PRECOMPILED_HEADERS "Precompile the common headers of the largest contrib libraries" ${ENABLE_PRECOMPILED_HEADERS})
+
+set (CLICKHOUSE_PCH_HEADERS
+    algorithm array atomic bit cassert cctype cerrno cfloat climits clocale cmath compare cstddef cstdint cstdio
+    cstdlib cstring ctime cwchar cwctype deque exception functional initializer_list iosfwd iterator limits map
+    memory mutex new numeric optional ratio set source_location span stdexcept string string_view system_error
+    tuple type_traits typeinfo unordered_map unordered_set utility variant vector version
+    fmt/format.h magic_enum.hpp
+    # Third-party headers included by most sources: vendored Poco, boost, cityhash, double-conversion.
+    Poco/Exception.h boost/core/noncopyable.hpp boost/noncopyable.hpp boost/smart_ptr/intrusive_ptr.hpp city.h

+# clickhouse_target_precompiled_headers (target [SKIP_TARGET_DIR_SOURCES] {HEADERS header... | REUSE_FROM other_target})
+# SKIP_TARGET_DIR_SOURCES: sources in the target's own CMake directory (for contrib: stubs, generated parsers and
+# version files kept next to contrib/<library>-cmake/CMakeLists.txt) are compiled as before.
+function (clickhouse_target_precompiled_headers target)
+    cmake_parse_arguments (PCH "SKIP_TARGET_DIR_SOURCES" "REUSE_FROM" "HEADERS" ${ARGN})
+    if (PCH_REUSE_FROM)
+        target_precompile_headers (${target} REUSE_FROM ${PCH_REUSE_FROM})
+    else ()
+        set (headers)
+        foreach (header IN LISTS PCH_HEADERS)
+            list (APPEND headers "$<$<COMPILE_LANGUAGE:CXX>:<${header}$<ANGLE-R>>")
+        endforeach ()
+        target_precompile_headers (${target} PRIVATE ${headers})
+    endif ()
+    # Keep template instantiation in the translation units, so the generated code does not change.
+    set_target_properties (${target} PROPERTIES PCH_INSTANTIATE_TEMPLATES OFF)
+
+    get_target_property (source_dir ${target} SOURCE_DIR)
+    get_target_property (binary_dir ${target} BINARY_DIR)
+    get_target_property (sources ${target} SOURCES)
+    foreach (source IN LISTS sources)
+        if (source MATCHES "^\\$<" OR NOT source MATCHES "\\.(cpp|cc|cxx)$")
+            continue ()
+        endif ()
+        # Resolve like CMake does: relative to the target's source directory, else its binary directory (generated files).
+        if (IS_ABSOLUTE "${source}")
+            set (path "${source}")
+        elseif (EXISTS "${source_dir}/${source}")
+            set (path "${source_dir}/${source}")
+        else ()
+            set (path "${binary_dir}/${source}")
+        endif ()
+        if (PCH_SKIP_TARGET_DIR_SOURCES)
+            string (FIND "${path}" "${source_dir}/" pos)
+            if (pos EQUAL 0)
+                set_source_files_properties ("${path}" TARGET_DIRECTORY ${target} PROPERTIES SKIP_PRECOMPILE_HEADERS ON)
+                continue ()
+            endif ()
+        endif ()
+        foreach (property COMPILE_FLAGS COMPILE_OPTIONS COMPILE_DEFINITIONS)
+            get_source_file_property (value "${path}" TARGET_DIRECTORY ${target} ${property})
+            if (value)
+                set_source_files_properties ("${path}" TARGET_DIRECTORY ${target} PROPERTIES SKIP_PRECOMPILE_HEADERS ON)
+                break ()
+            endif ()
+        endforeach ()
+    endforeach ()
+
+    get_target_property (launcher ${target} CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER)
+    list (FILTER launcher INCLUDE REGEX "(^|/)ccache$")
+    if (launcher)
+        execute_process (COMMAND ${launcher} --get-config sloppiness
+            OUTPUT_VARIABLE sloppiness OUTPUT_STRIP_TRAILING_WHITESPACE ERROR_QUIET RESULT_VARIABLE rc)
+        if (NOT rc EQUAL 0)
+            set (sloppiness "")
+        endif ()
+        string (REPLACE " " "" sloppiness "${sloppiness},pch_defines,time_macros")
+        string (REGEX REPLACE "^," "" sloppiness "${sloppiness}")
+        get_target_property (launcher ${target} CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER)
+        set_target_properties (${target} PROPERTIES CXX_COMPILER_LAUNCHER "env;CCACHE_SLOPPINESS=${sloppiness};${launcher}")
+    endif ()
+endfunction ()

+function (clickhouse_add_precompiled_headers)
+    if (NOT ENABLE_PRECOMPILED_HEADERS)
+        return ()
+    endif ()
+
+    foreach (target IN LISTS CLICKHOUSE_PCH_TARGETS)
+        if (TARGET ${target})
+            clickhouse_target_precompiled_headers (${target} HEADERS ${CLICKHOUSE_PCH_HEADERS})
+        endif ()
+    endforeach ()
+
+    if (NOT ENABLE_CONTRIB_PRECOMPILED_HEADERS)
+        return ()
+    endif ()
+
+    if (TARGET _aws)
+        clickhouse_target_precompiled_headers (_aws SKIP_TARGET_DIR_SOURCES HEADERS ${CLICKHOUSE_CONTRIB_PCH_HEADERS__aws})
+    endif ()
+    if (TARGET grpc)
+        clickhouse_target_precompiled_headers (grpc SKIP_TARGET_DIR_SOURCES HEADERS ${CLICKHOUSE_CONTRIB_PCH_HEADERS_grpc})
+    endif ()
+    if (TARGET _rocksdb)
+        clickhouse_target_precompiled_headers (_rocksdb SKIP_TARGET_DIR_SOURCES HEADERS ${CLICKHOUSE_CONTRIB_PCH_HEADERS__rocksdb})
+    endif ()
+    # The LLVM libraries share their compile flags, so they share one PCH, built by LLVMCore. The libraries below the IR
+    # (and two YAML/DWARF readers) declare their own Argument, Value, Type, CallingConv or isDigit, which clash with the
+    # IR headers of that PCH, so they are compiled as before.
+    set (llvm_pch_exclude LLVMDemangle LLVMSupport LLVMBinaryFormat LLVMRemarks LLVMBitstreamReader LLVMTextAPI
+        LLVMTargetParser LLVMObjectYAML LLVMDebugInfoDWARF LLVMDebugInfoDWARFLowLevel)
+    if (TARGET LLVMCore)
+        clickhouse_target_precompiled_headers (LLVMCore SKIP_TARGET_DIR_SOURCES HEADERS ${CLICKHOUSE_CONTRIB_PCH_HEADERS_LLVM})
+        get_property (llvm_targets DIRECTORY "${ClickHouse_SOURCE_DIR}/contrib/llvm-project-cmake" PROPERTY BUILDSYSTEM_TARGETS)
+        foreach (target IN LISTS llvm_targets)
+            get_target_property (type ${target} TYPE)
+            if (target MATCHES "^LLVM" AND type STREQUAL "STATIC_LIBRARY" AND NOT target STREQUAL "LLVMCore"
+                AND NOT target IN_LIST llvm_pch_exclude)
+                clickhouse_target_precompiled_headers (${target} SKIP_TARGET_DIR_SOURCES REUSE_FROM LLVMCore)
+            endif ()
+        endforeach ()
+    endif ()
+    if (TARGET _mongocxx)
+        clickhouse_target_precompiled_headers (_mongocxx SKIP_TARGET_DIR_SOURCES HEADERS ${CLICKHOUSE_CONTRIB_PCH_HEADERS__mongocxx})
+    endif ()
```

issue.title: Skip mutation partition pruning when a predicate function is named like a column

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: ALTER UPDATE/DELETE and mutation execution over parts (including lightweight updates/deletes).

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Author is not a member of the ClickHouse organization

issue.body:
Part of #130256

### Changelog category (leave one):
- Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)

### Changelog entry (a user-readable short description of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Fixed partition pruning of mutations on ReplicatedMergeTree skipping a partition when the predicate contains a function named like a stored column, for example ``toYYYYMM(d) = 202401 AND `toYYYYMM(d)` = 7``. A mutation with such a predicate on a part where only some rows match is not covered by this change.

### Description
`MergeTreeData::getPartitionIdsPrunedByPredicate` builds the predicate DAG with plain names, so a stored column merges into any function node with the same name, whether or not the partition key computes it. `KeyCondition` then finds no distinct input to flag as colliding and prunes the wrong partition (`0 partition(s) affected`).

The change: return `std::nullopt` (no pruning) when a `FUNCTION` node of the predicate DAG has a `result_name` that names a storage column. This covers both `PARTITION BY toYYYYMM(d)` and `PARTITION BY d`. As with #130196, the trade-off is that such a predicate loses all pruning, including atoms that would prune safely. Pruning is kept where nothing collides, for example `DELETE WHERE d = '2024-01-01'` or a predicate on an `ALIAS` column.

Test: `05616_mutation_pruning_column_named_like_key_expression` covers both partition keys. It prints `0 1 1` on master and `0 0 0` with this change.

Not covered (execution side in `MutationsInterpreter`, to be fixed in a separate PR): the same predicate on a part where only some rows match, lightweight `DELETE FROM`, and `ALTER UPDATE` still behave incorrectly. They give the same result with `optimize_mutations_with_partition_pruning = 0`. Statistics part pruning in `SELECT` is also not covered.

issue.title: Do not execute addDate/addSeconds-family functions on NULL rows of Nullable(String)

labels.name: repo-f8f539ca
labels.description: Regular scalar functions: string processing, data conversion, arithmetic, math, comparison, condi...

issue.body:
Closes: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/issues/130381
Related: https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/pull/117359

### Changelog category (leave one):
- Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)

### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Fixed `addDate`, `subDate`, `addSeconds`, `addDays`, `subtractX`, `date_add` and the `+` / `-` operators with an `INTERVAL` throwing `CANNOT_PARSE_DATETIME` when the String argument is a `Nullable(String)` that contains NULL rows. Since 26.10 this also broke valid queries such as `addDate(formatDateTime(c1, ...), INTERVAL ...)` over a `Nullable(DateTime64)` (regression from #117359).

### Details

**Problem**

```sql
SELECT min(addDate(formatDateTime(c1, '%Y-%m-%d 00:00:00'), toIntervalSecond(0))) AS lo,
       max(addDate(formatDateTime(c1, '%Y-%m-%d 00:00:00'), toIntervalSecond(0))) AS hi
FROM (SELECT parseDateTime64BestEffortOrNull(arrayJoin(['2026-01-01 10:00:00', '']), 3, 'UTC') AS c1);
-- Code: 41. DB::Exception: CANNOT_PARSE_DATETIME
```

The `+` / `-` spelling fails the same way, for example `formatDateTime(c1, ...) + INTERVAL 0 SECOND` and `date_add(DAY, 1, formatDateTime(c1, ...))`.

**Cause**

Since #117359, `formatDateTime` declines `canBeExecutedOnDefaultArguments`, so it is no longer executed on the rows behind a NULL. Those rows are now filled with the default of the result type, the empty string. Before, they held `formatDateTime(default)`, which was `'1970-01-01 00:00:00'`.

The next function in the chain still accepts the contract, so it runs over the whole nested column, placeholder included, and tries to parse `''`. #117359 does what it promises. What broke is an accidental guarantee: the placeholder under a NULL used to be a parseable string by luck.

The plain `Nullable(String)` case is older: `addDate(x, ...)` and `addSeconds(x, 0)` over a `Nullable(String)` with a NULL already fail on 26.7 and 26.9, as measured by @groeneai. What #117359 changed is the `formatDateTime(...)` input and the `+ INTERVAL` shape.

The String is not parsed in `addDate` or in `plus` themselves. Both end up calling the `addSeconds`/`addDays`/... family, and the parsing happens in `FunctionDateOrDateTimeAddInterval`. The whole family is affected.

**Solution**

Three classes now decline `canBeExecutedOnDefaultArguments`, the same way `parseDateTime` does in #117359:

- `FunctionDateOrDateTimeAddInterval`: covers all `addX` / `subtractX`.
- `FunctionOpDate`: covers `addDate` / `subDate`. It needs its own override because `defaultImplementationForNulls` decides on the outermost function.
- `FunctionBinaryArithmetic` (`plus` / `minus`, also used by `date_add`): it strips the Nullable itself, so the two overrides above are not reached on this path. It declines only for `String +/- Interval`, using the argument types already known in the constructor (`prepared_interval_function`). The rest of the arithmetic is unchanged.

NULL rows are then filtered out before execution, and their result is masked as NULL anyway. `IFunction` is not changed: there is no cheap way to rebuild `f(default)` for the filtered rows, and the contract already says the value behind a NULL is not meaningful.

**Trade-off**

For `FunctionDateOrDateTimeAddInterval` and `FunctionOpDate` the hook has no access to the argument types, so a `Nullable(DateTime)` or `Nullable(Date)` input that contains NULLs also takes the filter, execute, expand path. Inputs without NULLs keep the fast path, because the filtering is keyed on the presence of a NULL (`anyArgumentHasNullRows`). The cost of the filtered path for date inputs with NULLs is not measured.

**Tests**

New test `05616_adddate_subdate_nullable_string_null_rows` covers:

- plain `Nullable(String)` and `LowCardinality(Nullable(String))` with a NULL, for `addDate`, `subDate`, `addSeconds` and `subtractDays`;
- `x + INTERVAL`, `x - INTERVAL` and `INTERVAL + x` on `Nullable(String)`, and `x + INTERVAL` on `LowCardinality(Nullable(String))`;
- the query from the issue, with and without `compatibility = '24.12'`, and `addSeconds`, `+ INTERVAL`, `- INTERVAL` and `date_add` variants over `formatDateTime(...)`;
- `Nullable(Date)` with a NULL, to check the filtered path on date arguments;
- inputs without NULLs.

comment.body:
I looked at the new head (`3804e897`).

1. `8d8523b6` put the change into the wrong file. It replaced all of `src/Functions/FunctionDateOrDateTimeAddInterval.h` with a copy of `FunctionBinaryArithmetic.h` plus your three lines (that is the +4457/-1040). `FunctionBinaryArithmetic.h` itself is not changed in the PR, and the `FunctionDateOrDateTimeAddInterval` class, together with your first override, is gone, so the head does not build:

```
src/Functions/addSeconds.cpp:8:28: error: no template named 'FunctionDateOrDateTimeAddInterval'
```

To fix it: `git checkout 1cd7a9a6f8f9 -- src/Functions/FunctionDateOrDateTimeAddInterval.h` (that version is current master plus your 8-line override, nothing else), then apply the three hunks (the `parses_string_operand` member, the line after `prepared_interval_function = ...` in the constructor, and the `canBeExecutedOnDefaultArguments` change) to `src/Functions/FunctionBinaryArithmetic.h`.

2. With the change in the right place the approach works. I built master `2b6c3dd9b6b9` with your two overrides plus those three hunks in `FunctionBinaryArithmetic.h`. Your test output matches the `.reference` (run with `clickhouse local`), and the four queries from my previous comment plus the issue query all return values. On a master build without the change, 16 of the test's queries and all five of those throw `CANNOT_PARSE_DATETIME`. A non-NULL row that is not a date (`'garbage'`) still throws, so only the NULL rows are skipped.

   One correction to my previous comment: `plus` does use the default implementation for NULLs, but that path checks `plus`'s own `canBeExecutedOnDefaultArguments`, not the one on `addX`. That is why the override has to be on `plus`, as you did.

3. The changelog entry now says which part regressed. That reads right to me.

I still have not measured the cost of the filtered path.

<!-- rp:874c83e013374e45ae064cf703c525b3 -->

A 256-bit mask has to be cleared for every row, and that per-row 32-byte stack array is what made the arm speed depend on its alignment. So each entry holds a row stamp instead, and nothing is cleared between rows.

I tried `std::array<UInt8, 256>` stamps (cleared every 255 rows): same results, but on an x86 release build (1 thread, median of 30) it is slower than `UInt64` on longer strings and equal on short ones:

| strings | `UInt64` | `UInt8` |
|---|---|---|
| text, ~1 KB | 0.574 s | 0.604 s |
| random, 16 B | 0.250 s | 0.277 s |
| random, 256 B | 0.369 s | 0.379 s |

So I kept `UInt64` (2 KiB on the stack per call). If you prefer the smaller array anyway, I'll switch.

- Bug Fix (user-visible misbehavior in an official stable release)


### Changelog entry (a [user-readable short description](https://github.com/ClickHouse/ClickHouse/blob/master/docs/changelog_entry_guidelines.md) of the changes that goes into CHANGELOG.md):
Fixed `DeltaLake` queries hanging forever, without reacting to `KILL QUERY`, when delta-kernel could not create the thread that hands a result back (for example at a container PID limit).


### Description

On 26.3.12.3, a `DeltaLake` query hangs forever and ignores `KILL QUERY` when the server cannot create a new thread: in #128033 a `CREATE TABLE ... ENGINE = DeltaLake` run by `DDLWorker` blocked for 26 hours at a Kubernetes PID limit and stalled the distributed DDL queue. Master and 26.8 to 26.10 pin the same kernel code.

Cause: delta-kernel's `block_on` handed every result back through `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`. When no thread can be created, tokio panics after queueing the closure that owns the result sender, so the sender is never dropped and the caller's `recv()` waits forever. Every synchronous kernel call goes through `block_on`.

Change: `contrib/delta-kernel-rs` moves from `88ff5a94` to `86762ee5`, the merge commit of ClickHouse/delta-kernel-rs#19 (a cherry-pick of delta-io/delta-kernel-rs#3202), which sends the result directly from the async task. It touches only `kernel/src/engine/default/executor.rs`, with no Cargo manifest or lock change. The fork branch tip carries unrelated changes, so the pin is the fix commit, not the tip.

Validation: a standalone kernel program that lowers `RLIMIT_NPROC` before calling `block_on` hangs on `88ff5a94` (panic `OS can't spawn worker thread`, caller blocked in `futex_wait`) and returns the result on `86762ee5`, in 6 of 6 runs each. The server builds with the new pin, and 59 local DeltaLake stateless tests pass. No ClickHouse test is added: running a server out of threads at exactly this point is not deterministic in a functional test.

#130062 moves the pointer to `c694ca3e`, which already contains this commit.
